analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $26.59 by 2030, then recalculates it every seven years.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the federal minimum wage in steps to $26.59 an hour by 2030 has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no hearing and no cosponsors since its introduction on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage — which has been stuck at $7.25 an hour since 2009 — to $10.59 in 2026, then by $4 each year until it reaches $26.59 in 2030. After that, the Labor Department would set the wage every seven years at the level that lets a worker putting in about 35 hours a week earn at least 40% above the poverty line for a family of four, with no rule allowing the wage to go down. States could still set higher minimum wages. The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly tens of millions of workers who earn near the federal minimum — disproportionately women, part-time and service workers, and workers in the many states that use the federal $7.25 floor — would see their pay rise in scheduled steps. Families earning the minimum would gain a clearer path to affording rent and basic needs; the bill's own findings cite poverty rates and housing costs as the problem it addresses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum-wage workers, especially in low-wage states

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10.59 on January 1, 2026, then by $4 annually until it reaches $26.59 on January 1, 2030.

After 2030, the Labor Department must set the wage every seven years so that a person working 1,799 hours a year (about 35 hours a week) earns 40% above the federal supplemental poverty threshold for a renting family of four with two children — and may never lower the wage below the rate in effect.
The bill leaves states, cities, and tribes free to set higher minimum wages than the federal floor.

The bill's findings state that a full-time minimum-wage worker earns just $20 above the poverty line for a single person, and that average rent for a one-bedroom apartment exceeds 110% of such a worker's monthly income.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay wages near the federal minimum — heavily restaurants, retail, hospitality, agriculture, and franchise chains — would face stepped-up labor costs through 2030, with some costs passed to consumers as higher prices and some felt in reduced hiring or hours where margins are thinnest. Small businesses operating on minimum-wage labor would bear more of the adjustment burden than large firms that already pay above $10.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other minimum-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The step-up is steep: wages more than triple from $7.25 to $26.59 in five years, which low-wage employers argue would force price increases, cut hours, or accelerate automation in industries like restaurants and retail that run on thin margins.

The formula resets the wage only every seven years based on a poverty-measure benchmark, so between resets the wage would not track inflation; a period of high inflation after 2030 could erode the real value of the wage until the next adjustment.
A single national wage floor applies the same rate in high-cost and low-cost regions, which some economists say hits small businesses in low-cost areas harder than big firms in expensive cities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers earning near $7.25, the gains are direct and large — a nearly fourfold raise in pay over five years, tied to a housing-and-poverty benchmark. The cost side is real but standard for any minimum wage increase: higher labor costs for employers, some passed to consumers, with the intensity of the debate coming from the unusually steep pace and the high target of $26.59. The bill does not include small-business phase-ins or regional exceptions, which makes the adjustment harsher for thin-margin employers than a slower schedule would be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on January 3, 2025, and has had no hearing, no markup, and no floor action since — with zero cosponsors signed on, it is effectively sitting untouched while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Representative Al Green of Texas introduced the bill on January 3, 2025.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce the same day, which is where minimum wage legislation sits unless the committee schedules a hearing or markup.
No member has cosponsored the bill, and the action history shows no further steps since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that pay at or near the federal minimum wage are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced and the current $7.25 floor remains in place.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Original LAW Act and referred to it as a way to tie the minimum wage to a poverty-and-housing benchmark.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled in more than a year of the 119th Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the floor; with the chamber under Republican control and no committee action, no vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no votes, so no partisan split can be measured from the record; minimum wage legislation generally divides along party lines.

industries.industry: Restaurants, hospitality, and other minimum-wage employers
industries.note: These industries would face sharply higher labor costs as the wage climbs to $26.59 by 2030; their interest in keeping the $7.25 floor runs against the wage gains the bill promises workers.
Tens of millions of workers near the minimum would see pay rise in scheduled steps, which is the bill's core purpose.

They would bear the wage increase too, but many already pay above $10, so the adjustment burden falls relatively harder on small competitors — some large chains have historically supported minimum wage increases for that reason.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action in over a year, and a Republican House majority that has not brought minimum wage legislation to the floor, the realistic path is that the bill dies in committee when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. A standalone minimum wage increase of this size is very unlikely to move in this Congress.
